common_name: Fifth of July Hibiscus (Multicolor Red-Orange-Yellow Tropical Hibiscus)

planting.note: Root softwood cuttings or set out container plants once nights stay reliably above 50°F; Fifth of July is prized among exotic hibiscus collectors for its swirling blend of red, orange, and gold on a single ruffled bloom.

directions: Grow Fifth of July in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade, where the strongest light brings out the sharpest contrast between its red base color and orange-to-yellow petal edges. Each flower opens for only a single day and can shift subtly in color intensity from morning to afternoon as temperatures rise, a trait common to many of the modern exotic hibiscus hybrids. Pinch young plants to encourage branching and deadhead spent blooms to keep the shrub tidy, feeding every few weeks during the growing season with a bloom-formulated fertilizer to sustain its continuous flowering habit. Bring container specimens indoors to a bright window before the first frost, since this cultivar has no cold hardiness.

common_name: Cajun Cocktail Hibiscus (Ruffled Red-Orange-Yellow Blend Tropical Hibiscus)

planting.note: Plant container specimens or rooted cuttings after all danger of frost has passed; Cajun Cocktail produces heavily ruffled flowers that blend fiery red, orange, and yellow tones around a deep maroon throat.

directions: Site Cajun Cocktail in rich, well-drained soil with full morning sun and some protection from the hottest afternoon rays, which helps the layered petal colors hold their vibrancy longer through the day. The heavily crimped, wavy-edged petals give each bloom a livelier, more textured look than flat-flowered hibiscus cultivars, though as with all tropical hibiscus each flower lasts only a single day. Water deeply whenever the top inch of soil dries out and apply a balanced, slow-release fertilizer through the warm months to keep new flower buds forming continuously. In climates with any winter chill, grow it in a container that can be moved to a sheltered, bright spot once temperatures drop.

common_name: Ross Estey Hibiscus (Large Pale Peach-Pink Tropical Hibiscus)

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or nursery plants once nighttime temperatures stay reliably above 50°F; Ross Estey is a long-grown Hawaiian-bred cultivar valued for its enormous, softly ruffled peach-pink single blooms.

directions: Plant Ross Estey in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, giving it plenty of room since it grows into a large, vigorous shrub over time. Its flowers rank among the largest of the classic single-form tropical hibiscus, opening a delicate pale peach-pink with a slightly deeper blush toward the throat, and appearing in flushes throughout the warm months. Prune after the main flowering flush to control size and stimulate fresh branching, since blooms form on new growth. Protect the plant from temperatures below 40°F, moving container specimens indoors well ahead of any cold snap.
sources: University of Hawaii College of Tropical Agriculture and Human Resources

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant after all frost danger has passed; Rosalie is a bushier, more compact roselle selection bred to set a heavier crop of thick red calyces on a smaller frame than older tall roselle strains.

directions: Sow Rosalie in warm, fertile soil after the soil has warmed well past 70°F, since roselle seedlings are frost-tender and slow to establish in cool conditions. This selection branches low and fills out into a dense, rounded bush that carries a heavier concentration of plump, deep red calyces per plant than taller heirloom roselle types, making it a good fit for smaller vegetable beds or large containers. Like other roselle, it is day-length sensitive and begins setting flowers and calyces as days shorten in late summer, so harvest continues from late summer until frost. Pick the fleshy calyces about a week after the petals fall, while still tender, for fresh use, drying, or syrup.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Roselle (Hibiscus sabdariffa)

planting.note: Direct sow after the soil has warmed or start indoors 4-6 weeks before transplanting out; Red Zinger is the roselle strain long associated with the tart, ruby-red herbal tea blend of the same name.

directions: Grow Red Zinger in full sun and warm, well-drained soil, spacing plants generously since the tall, reddish-stemmed bushes branch widely by late summer. It is a short-day plant that holds off flowering until the days begin to shorten in late summer, then quickly loads its branches with the thick, tart, deep-red calyces that give the tea blend bearing its name its characteristic color and tang. Harvest calyces within a week or two after the petals drop, while they are still crisp, since they toughen and lose quality if left too long on the plant. Dry the harvested calyces thoroughly for tea, or use fresh for syrups, jams, and sauces before the first frost ends the season.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Roselle (Hibiscus sabdariffa)
